questions.question: What is the full form of GMO?
questions.explanation: GMO stands for Genetically Modified Organism, which refers to plants, bacteria, fungi, and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation.

questions.question: Which of the following abiotic stresses can GM crops be made more tolerant to?
questions.explanation: Genetic modification has made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses including cold, drought, salt, and heat.

questions.question: Golden rice is an example of GM crop enriched with which vitamin?
questions.explanation: Golden rice is a Vitamin A enriched rice, which is an example of enhanced nutritional value through genetic modification.

questions.question: Bt toxin is produced by which bacterium?
questions.explanation: Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis, commonly abbreviated as Bt.

questions.question: Why does Bt toxin not kill the Bacillus bacteria itself?
options: Because bacteria are resistant to the toxin
Because the toxin exists as inactive protoxin in the bacteria
Because bacteria enclose toxin in a special sac
questions.explanation: The Bt toxin protein exists as inactive protoxins in the bacteria. It is only converted to active form when ingested by insects due to the alkaline pH of their gut.

questions.question: What causes the conversion of inactive Bt protoxin to active toxin in insects?
options: Acidic pH of the insect gut
Alkaline pH of the insect gut
High temperature in the insect body
questions.explanation: The alkaline pH of the insect gut solubilizes the crystals and converts the inactive protoxin into active toxin.

questions.question: After activation, how does Bt toxin kill the insect?
options: By blocking the insect's nervous system
By binding to midgut epithelial cells and creating pores
By producing toxic gases in the gut
questions.explanation: The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis, eventually causing death.

questions.question: Which cry genes control cotton bollworms?
questions.explanation: The proteins encoded by genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, while cryIAb controls corn borer.

questions.question: Which insect groups are killed by Bt toxin proteins?
questions.explanation: Some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce proteins that kill lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).

questions.question: How do GM pest-resistant plants help reduce environmental harm?
options: By reducing reliance on chemical pesticides
questions.explanation: Genetic modification has reduced reliance on chemical pesticides through pest-resistant crops, thereby minimizing harmful effects on the environment.

questions.question: How does genetic modification help in maintaining soil fertility?
options: By adding more minerals to soil
By increasing efficiency of mineral usage by plants
questions.explanation: GM plants have increased efficiency of mineral usage, which prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility.

questions.question: Bt cotton is an example of which type of crop?
options: Hybrid crop produced by traditional breeding
questions.explanation: Bt cotton is a genetically modified crop where Bt toxin genes from Bacillus thuringiensis have been incorporated into cotton plants.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of genetic modification in agriculture?
questions.explanation: Genetic modification has helped to reduce post-harvest losses, which is one of the important benefits of GM crops.

questions.question: What is created when Bt toxin gene is expressed in plants?
questions.explanation: When Bt toxin gene is cloned and expressed in plants, it creates a bio-pesticide that provides resistance to insects without chemical insecticides.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a Bt crop in the text?
questions.explanation: The text mentions Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato, and soyabean as examples, but not Bt wheat.

questions.question: What does the prefix 'cry' in cryIAc and cryIIAb stand for?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'cry' refers to crystal protein genes that code for the insecticidal crystal proteins produced by Bacillus thuringiensis.

questions.question: Besides food production, GM has been used to supply alternative resources to industries in the form of:
questions.explanation: GM has been used to create tailor-made plants to supply alternative resources to industries in the form of starches, fuels, and pharmaceuticals.

questions.question: During which phase of growth does B. thuringiensis form protein crystals?
options: During a particular phase of their growth
questions.explanation: B. thuringiensis forms protein crystals during a particular phase of their growth, which contain the toxic insecticidal protein.

questions.question: How is the choice of Bt toxin genes determined for different crops?
options: Based on the crop and the targeted pest
Based only on the crop type
questions.explanation: The choice of genes depends upon the crop and the targeted pest, as most Bt toxins are insect-group specific.

questions.question: The cryIAb gene controls which pest?
questions.explanation: The protein encoded by cryIAb controls corn borer, while cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms.

questions.question: What happens to Bt protoxin when it enters an insect's gut?
options: It is destroyed by stomach acids
It is converted to active toxin by alkaline pH
questions.explanation: Once an insect ingests the inactive toxin, it is converted into an active form due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilizes the crystals.

questions.question: How many major benefits of GM plants are listed in the text?
questions.explanation: The text lists five major benefits: tolerance to abiotic stresses, reduced reliance on pesticides, reduced post-harvest losses, increased mineral usage efficiency, and enhanced nutritional value.

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of lepidopterans targeted by Bt toxin?
questions.explanation: Lepidopterans include tobacco budworm and armyworm, while beetles are coleopterans and flies/mosquitoes are dipterans.

questions.question: What is presented as a possible solution to minimize harmful effects of fertilizers and chemicals on the environment?
questions.explanation: Use of genetically modified crops is presented as a possible solution to minimize the use of fertilizers and chemicals and reduce their harmful effects.

questions.question: Which organisms can be classified as GMOs according to the text?
questions.explanation: Plants, bacteria, fungi, and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called Genetically Modified Organisms.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an application of biotechnology in the chapter introduction?
questions.explanation: The text lists applications of biotechnology as therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, and energy production. Space exploration is not mentioned.

questions.question: What does biotechnology essentially deal with according to the chapter introduction?
options: Industrial scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified organisms
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that biotechnology essentially deals with industrial scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants and animals.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as the first critical research area of biotechnology?
options: Providing the best catalyst in the form of improved organism usually a microbe or pure enzyme
questions.explanation: The three critical research areas are listed as: (i) providing the best catalyst in the form of improved organism usually a microbe or pure enzyme, (ii) creating optimal conditions through engineering, and (iii) downstream processing technologies.

questions.question: The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply but was still not enough because of what reason?
options: The food was of poor quality
It was not enough to feed the growing human population
questions.explanation: The text states that the Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply but yet it was not enough to feed the growing human population.

questions.question: What is the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant called?
questions.explanation: The text defines totipotency as the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant. Micro-propagation is the method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture.

questions.question: Which part of a plant is taken out and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions in tissue culture?
questions.explanation: The text states that whole plants could be regenerated from explants, which is any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions in special nutrient media.

questions.question: What are the plants produced through micro-propagation called?
questions.explanation: The text states that each of these plants produced through micro-propagation will be genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown, and they are called somaclones.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a component of the nutrient medium for tissue culture?
options: Growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins
questions.explanation: The text mentions that the nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose and also inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins. Antibiotics are not mentioned.

questions.question: What is the term for isolated naked protoplasts obtained after digesting plant cell walls?
questions.explanation: The text states that after digesting cell walls, scientists have been able to isolate naked protoplasts surrounded by plasma membranes.

questions.question: What is the hybrid plant produced by fusing tomato and potato protoplasts called?
questions.explanation: The text mentions that when a protoplast of tomato is fused with that of potato and grown, it results in the formation of pomato.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as the third option for increasing food production?
questions.explanation: The three options listed for increasing food production are: (i) agro-chemical based agriculture, (ii) organic agriculture, and (iii) genetically engineered crop-based agriculture.

questions.question: What is the process called when isolated protoplasts from two different plant varieties are fused?
questions.explanation: The text defines somatic hybridisation as the process where isolated protoplasts from two different varieties of plants are fused to get hybrid protoplasts, which can be grown to form a new plant.

questions.question: Which growth regulators are specifically mentioned as components of the tissue culture medium?
questions.explanation: The text specifically mentions growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins as components of the nutrient medium for tissue culture.

questions.question: Why can virus-free plants be obtained from meristem culture even if the plant is infected with a virus?
options: Because viruses cannot enter the meristem
Because the meristem is free of virus
Because viruses are killed in the meristem
Because meristem cells are resistant to viruses
questions.explanation: The text states that even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus, hence virus-free plants can be obtained by removing and growing the meristem in vitro.

questions.question: Why does the Bt toxin not kill the Bacillus thuringiensis bacteria itself?
options: The bacteria are naturally resistant to all toxins
The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin in the bacteria
The bacteria enclose the toxin in a protective sac
The bacterial cell wall prevents toxin entry
questions.explanation: The Bt toxin protein exists as inactive protoxins in Bacillus thuringiensis. It only becomes active when ingested by an insect, where the alkaline pH of the gut solubilizes the crystals and converts it into an active toxin.

questions.question: What happens when the activated Bt toxin binds to the midgut epithelial cells of an insect?
options: It creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis
It triggers an immune response in the insect
It destroys the insect's nervous system
questions.explanation: The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores. This causes cell swelling and lysis, eventually leading to the death of the insect.

questions.question: Which of the following groups of insects is NOT mentioned as being killed by Bt toxin proteins?
questions.explanation: The text mentions that Bt toxin proteins kill lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes). Hymenopterans are not mentioned in the text.

questions.question: Which cry genes are mentioned as controlling cotton bollworms?
questions.explanation: The proteins encoded by genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, while cryIAb controls corn borer.

questions.question: What determines the choice of Bt toxin genes to be incorporated into crop plants?
options: The soil type where the crop is grown
The crop species and the targeted pest
questions.explanation: The choice of genes depends upon the crop and the targeted pest, as most Bt toxins are insect-group specific.

questions.question: In RNA interference (RNAi), what causes the silencing of specific mRNA?
options: A single-stranded RNA molecule binding to mRNA
A protein enzyme that degrades mRNA
A DNA molecule that replaces the mRNA
questions.explanation: RNAi involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA.

questions.question: Which nematode is mentioned as infecting tobacco plants and causing reduction in yield?
questions.explanation: Meloidogyne incognitia is the nematode that infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield.

questions.question: What is the source of complementary RNA that initiates RNAi in eukaryotic organisms?
options: From viruses with RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons)
questions.explanation: The source of complementary RNA could be from an infection by viruses having RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.

questions.question: How are nematode-specific genes introduced into the host plant to create pest resistance?
options: Through direct injection into plant leaves
By spraying a chemical solution on the plant
questions.explanation: Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant to produce both sense and anti-sense RNA.

questions.question: What is formed when sense RNA and anti-sense RNA, being complementary to each other, come together in the host cells?
questions.explanation: Sense and anti-sense RNA being complementary to each other form a double-stranded (dsRNA) that initiates RNAi and silences the specific mRNA of the nematode.

questions.question: What is the consequence of RNAi in the transgenic host plant expressing specific interfering RNA?
options: The plant becomes more susceptible to the nematode
The parasite cannot survive in the transgenic host
The plant grows faster than normal
The nematode develops resistance to the plant
questions.explanation: The parasite could not survive in a transgenic host expressing specific interfering RNA, so the transgenic plant gets itself protected from the parasite.

questions.question: What condition in the insect gut is responsible for converting the inactive Bt protoxin into its active form?
options: Alkaline pH of the gut that solubilizes the crystals
questions.explanation: The inactive toxin is converted into an active form due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilizes the crystals. The activated toxin then binds to midgut cells.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of recombinant therapeutics over products isolated from non-human sources?
options: They are less expensive to produce
They do not induce unwanted immunological responses
They can be stored at room temperature
questions.explanation: Recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses as is common in case of similar products isolated from non-human sources.

questions.question: How many recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use worldwide according to the text?
questions.explanation: At present, about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human-use the world over.

questions.question: From which animal sources was insulin historically extracted before recombinant DNA technology?
questions.explanation: Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.

questions.question: What problem did some patients develop when using insulin from animal sources?
options: They developed allergy or reactions to the foreign protein
questions.explanation: Insulin from an animal source, though caused some patients to develop allergy or other types of reactions to the foreign protein.

questions.question: Insulin consists of how many polypeptide chains and what are they called?
options: One polypeptide chain called the insulin chain
Two polypeptide chains called chain A and chain B
Three polypeptide chains called A, B, and C
Four polypeptide chains called alpha, beta, gamma, and delta
questions.explanation: Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains: chain A and chain B, that are linked together by disulphide bridges.

questions.question: What is the extra stretch present in the pro-hormone form of insulin called?
questions.explanation: In mammals, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide. This C peptide is not present in the mature insulin.

questions.question: What was the main challenge in producing insulin using recombinant DNA techniques?
options: Getting insulin assembled into a mature form
Obtaining the DNA sequences from human cells
questions.explanation: The main challenge for production of insulin using rDNA techniques was getting insulin assembled into a mature form.

questions.question: In 1983, what did Eli Lilly company do to produce human insulin using bacteria?
options: They extracted insulin directly from human pancreas
They prepared two DNA sequences for A and B chains and introduced them into E.coli plasmids
They synthesized insulin chemically in the laboratory
They used yeast cells instead of bacteria
questions.explanation: In 1983, Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them in plasmids of E.coli to produce insulin chains.

questions.question: What is gene therapy fundamentally attempting to achieve?
options: To replace all genes in a person's body
To correct a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child or embryo
To create new species of organisms
To eliminate all genetic diseases from the population
questions.explanation: Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child or embryo. Here genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease.

questions.question: What was the first clinical gene therapy given in 1990 used to treat?
questions.explanation: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. This enzyme is crucial for the immune system to function.

questions.question: What causes ADA deficiency disorder?
options: Deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase
questions.explanation: The disorder is caused due to the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase. This enzyme is crucial for the immune system to function.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a treatment approach for ADA deficiency?
questions.explanation: The text mentions bone marrow transplantation, enzyme replacement therapy, and gene therapy using lymphocytes. Radiation therapy is not mentioned.

questions.question: Why does the patient require periodic infusion of genetically engineered lymphocytes in ADA gene therapy?
options: Because the lymphocytes are rejected by the immune system
Because these cells are not immortal and die over time
Because the retroviral vector becomes inactive
Because the ADA enzyme breaks down quickly
questions.explanation: As these cells are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes.

questions.question: What could be a permanent cure for ADA deficiency according to the text?
options: Repeated bone marrow transplants throughout life
Introducing the gene from marrow cells into cells at early embryonic stages
Daily injections of functional ADA enzyme
Complete removal of the thymus gland
questions.explanation: If the gene isolate from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure.

questions.question: What defines a transgenic animal?
options: An animal with a naturally occurring genetic mutation
An animal whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express an extra foreign gene
An animal produced only through selective breeding
An animal with enhanced physical strength through genetic modification
questions.explanation: Transgenic animals are defined as animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene. This is achieved through recombinant DNA technology.

questions.question: What percentage of all existing transgenic animals are mice?
questions.explanation: The text states that although transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

questions.question: How do transgenic animals help in studying normal physiology and development?
options: By replacing all natural genes with synthetic ones
By introducing genes from other species to study biological effects of growth factors
By removing all growth factors from the animal
By preventing the animal from developing normally
questions.explanation: Transgenic animals are designed to study how genes are regulated and how they affect normal body functions and development. By introducing genes from other species that alter the formation of factors like insulin-like growth factor, scientists can study the resulting biological effects.

questions.question: Which of the following human diseases does NOT have a transgenic model mentioned in the text?
questions.explanation: The text mentions transgenic models exist for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease. Malaria is not mentioned as having a transgenic model.

questions.question: Which human protein produced in transgenic animals is used to treat emphysema?
questions.explanation: Transgenic animals can produce useful biological products such as human protein alpha-1-antitrypsin, which is used to treat emphysema. Similar attempts are being made for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis.

questions.question: What was special about the milk produced by the first transgenic cow Rosie in 1997?
options: It contained human alpha-lactalbumin (2.4g/L) and was nutritionally balanced for babies
It had a longer shelf life
questions.explanation: In 1997, the first transgenic cow Rosie produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre). The milk contained the human alpha-lactalbumin and was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk.

questions.question: Which transgenic animal is being developed to test the safety of the polio vaccine?
questions.explanation: Transgenic mice are being developed for use in testing the safety of vaccines before they are used on humans. They are specifically being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine and could replace the use of monkeys.

questions.question: What makes transgenic animals particularly useful for chemical safety testing?
options: They are immune to all toxic substances
They carry genes making them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals
They can break down toxins faster
They do not require ethical approval
questions.explanation: Transgenic animals are made to carry genes which make them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals. They are exposed to toxic substances and the effects are studied, allowing results to be obtained in less time.

questions.question: Why does the text state that manipulation of living organisms cannot continue without regulation?
options: Because genetic modification can have unpredictable results when introduced into the ecosystem
Because it requires too much laboratory space
Because animals do not survive the process
questions.explanation: The text states that genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem. Therefore, ethical standards and regulatory bodies like GEAC are needed to evaluate the morality and safety of such activities.

questions.question: What is the full form of GEAC mentioned in the text?
questions.explanation: GEAC stands for Genetic Engineering Approval Committee. It was set up by the Indian Government to make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services.

questions.question: What happened in 1997 regarding Basmati rice that caused concern?
options: India banned all exports of Basmati rice
An American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office
All Basmati varieties were genetically modified
questions.explanation: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office. This allowed them to sell a 'new' variety derived from Indian farmers' varieties, claiming it as an invention.

questions.question: What is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies without proper authorization and compensatory payment?
questions.explanation: Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment.

questions.question: According to the text, how do industrialized nations and developing countries differ in terms of biodiversity and traditional knowledge?
options: Industrialized nations are rich in both biodiversity and traditional knowledge
Developing countries are rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while industrialized nations are poor in these but rich financially
Both have equal levels of biodiversity and financial resources
Developing countries have no traditional knowledge
questions.explanation: The text states that most industrialized nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. In contrast, the developing and underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.

questions.question: What legislative action has India taken to address issues related to biopiracy and patents?
options: Banned all foreign companies from operating in India
Cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill considering patent terms, emergency provisions, and R&D initiatives
questions.explanation: The Indian Parliament has recently cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, that takes issues like biopiracy into consideration, including patent terms of emergency provisions, research, and development initiatives.

questions.question: According to the chapter summary, what has biotechnology enabled humans to produce using microbes, plants, animals and their metabolic machinery?
questions.explanation: The summary states that biotechnology has given to humans several useful products by using microbes, plants, animals and their metabolic machinery.

questions.question: What potential do techniques of tissue culture and somatic hybridisation offer according to the summary?
options: They can only produce identical clones of existing plants
They offer vast potential for manipulation of plants in vitro to produce new varieties
They are only useful for producing virus-free plants
They can only be used on animal cells
questions.explanation: The summary states that techniques of tissue culture and somatic hybridisation offer vast potential for manipulation of plants in vitro to produce new varieties.

questions.question: What has recombinant DNA technology made possible according to the chapter summary?
options: Engineering microbes, plants and animals to have novel capabilities
Only DNA replication in test tubes
questions.explanation: The summary states that recombinant DNA technology has made it possible to engineer microbes, plants and animals such that they have novel capabilities.

questions.question: How are Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) created according to the summary?
options: By using methods other than natural methods to transfer one or more genes using recombinant DNA techniques
By selective breeding over many generations
questions.explanation: The summary states that GMOs have been created by using methods other than natural methods to transfer one or more genes from one organism to another, generally using techniques such as recombinant DNA techniques.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of GM plants in the summary?
options: Making crops more tolerant of stresses
questions.explanation: The summary mentions that GM plants have been useful in increasing crop yields, reducing postharvest losses and making crops more tolerant of stresses. Eliminating the need for sunlight is not mentioned.

questions.question: Why do recombinant therapeutics not induce unwanted immunological responses?
options: Because they are made from animal proteins
Because they are identical to human proteins
questions.explanation: The summary states that since recombinant therapeutics are identical to human proteins, they do not induce unwanted immunological responses and are free from risk of infection as was observed in case of similar products isolated from non-human sources.

questions.question: What is stated about human insulin produced using recombinant DNA technology?
options: It is different from natural insulin in structure
Its structure is absolutely identical to that of natural insulin
It is less effective than natural insulin
It causes more allergic reactions than animal insulin
questions.explanation: The summary explicitly states that human insulin is made in bacteria yet its structure is absolutely identical to that of the natural insulin.

questions.question: How do transgenic animals serve as models for human diseases according to the summary?
options: By being immune to all diseases
By understanding how genes contribute to disease development
By producing vaccines for human diseases
questions.explanation: The summary states that transgenic animals are used to understand how genes contribute to the development of a disease by serving as models for human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's.

questions.question: What is gene therapy according to the summary?
options: The removal of all defective genes from the body
The insertion of genes into an individual's cells and tissues to treat diseases especially hereditary diseases
The replacement of all cells in the body
The use of antibiotics to treat genetic disorders
questions.explanation: The summary defines gene therapy as the insertion of genes into an individual's cells and tissues to treat diseases especially hereditary diseases, by replacing a defective mutant allele with a functional one.

questions.question: What role do viruses play in gene therapy according to the summary?
options: They cause the disease being treated
They are used as vectors to transfer healthy genes or portions of genes
They are completely eliminated from the body
They are used to destroy defective genes
questions.explanation: The summary states that viruses that attack their hosts and introduce their genetic material into the host cell as part of their replication cycle are used as vectors to transfer healthy genes or more recently portions of genes.

questions.question: Which part of the plant is best suited for making virus-free plants and why?
options: Leaves because they have the highest chlorophyll content
Meristem (apical and axillary) because it is free of virus even if the plant is infected
Roots because they are underground and protected
Flowers because they have the most active cells
questions.explanation: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus. Hence one can remove the meristem and grow it in vitro to obtain virus-free plants.

questions.question: What is the major advantage of producing plants by micropropagation?
options: The plants are genetically different from the original plant
Thousands of genetically identical plants (somaclones) can be produced in very short durations
The plants grow much larger than normal
The plants do not require any nutrients
questions.explanation: Micropropagation is the method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture. Each plant will be genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown, i.e., they are somaclones. This allows propagation of a large number of plants in very short durations.

questions.question: Crystals of Bt toxin produced by some bacteria do not kill the bacteria themselves because?
options: Bacteria are resistant to the toxin
Bacteria enclose toxin in a special sac
questions.explanation: The Bt toxin protein exists as inactive protoxins in the bacteria. It only becomes active when an insect ingests the inactive toxin, where the alkaline pH of the gut solubilizes the crystals and converts it into an active toxin.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a component of the medium used for in vitro propagation of an explant?
questions.explanation: The nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose and also inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators like auxins, cytokinins etc. Antibiotics are not mentioned as a required component.

questions.question: How many varieties of rice are estimated to exist in India alone?
questions.explanation: The text states that there are an estimated 200,000 varieties of rice in India alone. This highlights the incredible diversity of rice in the country.

questions.question: What makes Basmati rice distinct from other rice varieties?
options: Its ability to grow in cold climates
questions.explanation: Basmati rice is distinct for its unique aroma and flavour. This characteristic has made it valuable and famous worldwide for centuries.

questions.question: How many documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India?
questions.explanation: The text mentions that 27 documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India. These varieties have been cultivated for centuries and referenced in ancient texts, folklore and poetry.

questions.question: In which year did an American company obtain patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office?
questions.explanation: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office. This was a significant event that raised concerns about biopiracy.

questions.question: What was the true origin of the 'new' Basmati variety patented by the American company?
options: It was developed entirely in American laboratories
It was derived from Indian farmer's varieties by crossing with semi-dwarf varieties
It was discovered growing wild in the United States
It was created through genetic modification using bacterial genes
questions.explanation: The 'new' variety of Basmati had actually been derived from Indian farmer's varieties. Indian Basmati was crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention or novelty.

questions.question: What does the patent extension to functional equivalents imply for Basmati rice sellers?
options: They can sell Basmati freely without any restrictions
Other people selling Basmati rice could be restricted by the patent
Only Indian farmers can sell Basmati rice
The patent only applies within the United States
questions.explanation: The patent extends to functional equivalents, implying that other people selling Basmati rice could be restricted by the patent. This creates a monopoly over a traditional Indian crop.

questions.question: Which traditional Indian herbal medicines have faced attempts to patent their uses, products and processes?
questions.explanation: Several attempts have been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines, such as turmeric and neem. These are part of India's rich traditional knowledge.

questions.question: What is biopiracy?
options: The illegal hunting of endangered animals
The use of bio-resources by multinational companies without proper authorisation and compensatory payment
The unauthorized release of genetically modified organisms into the environment
The theft of laboratory equipment from research institutions
questions.explanation: Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment.

questions.question: According to the text, what is the relationship between financial wealth and biodiversity in industrialized versus developing nations?
options: Industrialized nations are rich in both financial wealth and biodiversity
Developing nations are poor in both financial wealth and biodiversity
Industrialized nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity, while developing nations are the opposite
All nations have equal levels of financial wealth and biodiversity
questions.explanation: Most industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. In contrast, the developing and underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.

questions.question: How can traditional knowledge related to bio-resources be exploited for modern applications?
options: It can only be used for historical documentation
It can save time, effort and expenditure during commercialisation of modern applications
It has no value in modern science
It can only be used by indigenous communities
questions.explanation: Traditional knowledge related to bio-resources can be exploited to develop modern applications and can also be used to save time, effort and expenditure during their commercialisation.

questions.question: What growing realisation has emerged regarding the relationship between developed and developing countries in terms of bio-resources?
options: Developed countries should stop all research on bio-resources
There is injustice, inadequate compensation, and lack of benefit sharing between developed and developing countries
Developing countries have no valuable bio-resources
All bio-resources should be owned by international organizations
questions.explanation: There has been growing realisation of the injustice, inadequate compensation, and benefit sharing between developed and developing countries regarding the use of bio-resources and traditional knowledge.

questions.question: What recent legislative action has the Indian Parliament taken to address biopiracy and patent issues?
options: Banned all foreign companies from patenting Indian bio-resources
Cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill considering emergency provisions, research and development initiatives
Nationalized all traditional knowledge under government control
Eliminated the patent system completely in India
questions.explanation: The Indian Parliament has recently cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, that takes such issues into consideration, including patent terms of emergency provisions, research, and development initiatives.

questions.question: What is tissue culture in the context of plant biotechnology?
options: Growing whole plants from seeds in natural soil
Regenerating whole plants from explants grown in a test tube under sterile conditions in special nutrient media
Cross-breeding two different plant varieties to produce hybrids
Applying chemical fertilizers to enhance plant growth
questions.explanation: Tissue culture refers to the technique where whole plants can be regenerated from explants (any part of a plant taken out) and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions in special nutrient media. This was discovered by scientists during the 1950s.

questions.question: What is the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant called?
questions.explanation: The capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant is called totipotency. This is the fundamental principle behind tissue culture and micropropagation techniques.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a component of the nutrient medium for tissue culture?
questions.explanation: The nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins. Soil and natural sunlight are not mentioned as components of the nutrient medium for in vitro tissue culture.

questions.question: What is the method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture called?
questions.explanation: The method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture is called micropropagation. This method allows propagation of a large number of plants in very short durations.

questions.question: What are the plants produced through micropropagation called if they are genetically identical to the original plant?
questions.explanation: Each of the plants produced through micropropagation will be genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown. These are called somaclones.

questions.question: Which of the following food plants has been produced on commercial scale using micropropagation?
questions.explanation: Many important food plants like tomato, banana, apple, etc. have been produced on commercial scale using micropropagation.

questions.question: Why is the meristem preferred for producing virus-free plants through tissue culture?
options: Because it grows faster than other parts
Because it is free of virus even if the plant is infected
Because it is easier to extract
questions.explanation: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus. Hence, one can remove the meristem and grow it in vitro to obtain virus-free plants.

questions.question: Which plants have scientists succeeded in culturing meristems for virus-free propagation?
questions.explanation: Scientists have succeeded in culturing meristems of banana, sugarcane, and potato to produce virus-free plants through tissue culture.

questions.question: What are naked protoplasts?
options: Plant cells with thick cell walls
Plant cells surrounded by plasma membranes after cell wall digestion
questions.explanation: Scientists have isolated single cells from plants and after digesting their cell walls have been able to isolate naked protoplasts which are surrounded by plasma membranes.

questions.question: What is somatic hybridization?
options: Fusion of isolated protoplasts from two different plant varieties to form hybrid protoplasts
Grafting of two different plant stems
questions.explanation: Isolated protoplasts from two different varieties of plants, each having a desirable character, can be fused to get hybrid protoplasts, which can be further grown to form a new plant. This process is called somatic hybridization.

questions.question: What are the hybrids produced through somatic hybridization called?
questions.explanation: The hybrids produced through somatic hybridization are called somatic hybrids. An example mentioned is the pomato, formed by fusing tomato and potato protoplasts.

questions.question: What was the result of fusing tomato and potato protoplasts?
options: A commercially successful hybrid called pomato
A hybrid plant called pomato that did not have all desired characteristics for commercial use
A completely unsuccessful experiment with no plant formation
A new species of wild plant
questions.explanation: A protoplast of tomato fused with that of potato resulted in the formation of pomato. Unfortunately, this plant did not have all the desired combination of characteristics for its commercial utilization.

questions.question: What are the three options mentioned for increasing food production?
options: Agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture, and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture
Traditional farming, mechanized farming, and vertical farming
questions.explanation: The three options mentioned for increasing food production are: (i) agro-chemical based agriculture, (ii) organic agriculture, and (iii) genetically engineered crop-based agriculture.

questions.question: What was the main reason for the success of the Green Revolution in tripling food supply?
options: Mainly due to better management practices and use of agrochemicals
questions.explanation: Increased yields have partly been due to the use of improved crop varieties, but mainly due to the use of better management practices and use of agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides).

questions.question: Why did traditional breeding techniques fail to keep pace with demand for crop improvement?
options: They did not provide sufficiently fast and efficient systems
They only worked on fruit crops
questions.explanation: Traditional breeding techniques failed to keep pace with demand and to provide sufficiently fast and efficient systems for crop improvement, which led to the development of tissue culture technology.

questions.question: Which growth regulators are mentioned as components of the nutrient medium?
questions.explanation: The nutrient medium must provide growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins, along with a carbon source such as sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, and amino acids.

questions.question: What is an explant in tissue culture?
options: Any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions
A type of virus that infects plants
A growth hormone used in plant culture
questions.explanation: An explant is any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube under sterile conditions in special nutrient media. This was discovered by scientists during the 1950s.

questions.question: What is a major challenge for farmers in developing countries regarding agrochemicals?
options: They are too cheap and ineffective
They are banned by the government
They are only available in liquid form
questions.explanation: For farmers in the developing world, agrochemicals are often too expensive, and further increases in yield with existing varieties are not possible using conventional breeding alone.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key application of tissue culture mentioned in the text?
options: Recovery of healthy plants from diseased plants
questions.explanation: Another important application of the tissue culture method is the recovery of healthy plants from diseased plants. This is possible because the meristem is free of virus even if the plant is infected.

questions.question: What does the text suggest about further yield increases with existing crop varieties?
options: They can be achieved easily with more water
They are not possible using conventional breeding alone
They are unlimited with proper care
questions.explanation: The text states that further increases in yield with existing varieties are not possible using conventional breeding alone, which led to the development of tissue culture as an alternative technology.

questions.question: Which bacterium produces the Bt toxin used in genetically modified crops?
questions.explanation: Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium. The cry genes from this bacterium are inserted into crop plants to make them insect-resistant.

questions.question: Why does the Bt toxin not kill the Bacillus thuringiensis bacteria itself?
options: The bacteria are naturally resistant to the toxin
The toxin is enclosed in a special protective sac
The toxin exists as inactive protoxin in the bacteria
The bacteria have enzymes that destroy the toxin
questions.explanation: The Bt toxin protein exists as inactive protoxin in the bacteria. It becomes active only in the alkaline gut of insects after ingestion.

questions.question: What happens when an insect ingests the inactive Bt toxin?
options: It is immediately destroyed by stomach acids
It is converted to active toxin due to alkaline pH of the gut
It passes through the digestive system unchanged
It binds to bacterial cell walls
questions.explanation: Once an insect ingests the inactive toxin, it is converted into an active form due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilizes the crystals.

questions.question: The activated Bt toxin binds to which cells of the insect to cause death?
questions.explanation: The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis, leading to insect death.

questions.question: Which genes code for the Bt toxin proteins?
questions.explanation: The toxin is coded by genes named cry. Examples include cryIAc and cryIIAb which control cotton bollworms.

questions.question: Which cry genes control cotton bollworms?
questions.explanation: The proteins encoded by genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, while cryIAb controls corn borers.

questions.question: Which nematode infects the roots of tobacco plants and reduces yield?
questions.explanation: Meloidegyne incognitia is a nematode that parasitizes the roots of tobacco plants and causes great reduction in yield.

questions.question: What strategy is used to protect tobacco plants from Meloidegyne incognitia infestation?
questions.explanation: A novel strategy based on RNA interference (RNAi) is used. Nematode-specific genes are introduced into the host plant to produce dsRNA that silences nematode mRNA.

questions.question: What does RNAi stand for in the context of pest-resistant plants?
questions.explanation: RNAi stands for RNA Interference. It is a cellular defense method involving silencing of specific mRNA by complementary dsRNA.

questions.question: In RNAi, what type of RNA molecule binds to and prevents translation of the target mRNA?
questions.explanation: RNAi involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary double-stranded (dsRNA) molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA.

questions.question: How are nematode-specific genes introduced into the host plant for RNAi?
options: By direct injection into plant cells
questions.explanation: Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes are introduced into the host plant. The DNA produces both sense and antisense RNA.

questions.question: What happens when sense and antisense RNA are produced in the host plant cells?
questions.explanation: Sense and antisense RNA being complementary to each other form a double-stranded (dsRNA) that initiates RNAi and silences the specific mRNA of the nematode.

questions.question: What is the consequence of RNAi in transgenic plants against nematodes?
options: The parasite cannot survive in the transgenic host
The nematode becomes beneficial to the plant
questions.explanation: The parasite could not survive in a transgenic host expressing specific interfering RNA, thus the plant is protected from the parasite.

questions.question: Which insects are killed by proteins produced by some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis?
questions.explanation: Some strains of B. thuringiensis produce proteins that kill lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).

questions.question: During which phase of growth does Bacillus thuringiensis form protein crystals containing the toxin?
options: A particular phase of their growth
questions.explanation: B. thuringiensis forms protein crystals during a particular phase of their growth. These crystals contain the toxic insecticidal protein.

questions.question: What is the name of the process where isolated protoplasts from two different plant varieties are fused?
questions.explanation: Isolated protoplasts from two different varieties can be fused to get hybrid protoplasts. This process is called somatic hybridisation and the hybrids are called somatic hybrids.

questions.question: What is the term for plants regenerated from explants grown in test tubes under sterile conditions?
questions.explanation: Plants produced through micropropagation are genetically identical to the original plant and are called somaclones.

questions.question: Which part of a virus-infected plant is free of virus and can be used to produce virus-free plants?
questions.explanation: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus. Hence, meristem can be removed and grown in vitro to obtain virus-free plants.

questions.question: What is the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant called?
questions.explanation: The capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant is called totipotency. This property is utilized in tissue culture techniques.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a somatic hybrid produced through protoplast fusion?
questions.explanation: When a protoplast of tomato is fused with that of potato and grown, it forms pomato, a somatic hybrid combining tomato and potato characteristics.
